title: Choose FluidMusic’s new visual direction
question: Pick the clean operating system for the titlebar player and reduced Media workspace. Every option keeps native controls, provider truth, and stable playback across chats.

options.label: Public Radio Guide
options.lineage: public-radio schedules, programme guides, and continuity strips
options.thesis: FluidMusic reads like a calm live programme: the current source is unmistakable and Up Next follows as one continuous handoff.
options.viewport: A compact dark shell leads with the current programme strip, four task destinations, and a spacious provider workspace with no duplicate player footer.
options.risk: It becomes editorial rather than operational if headings grow too large or metadata loses alignment.

raised.raise: Every source and playback state receives one unambiguous wayfinding label.
Artwork earns scale only in Browse; controls stay quiet and compact.
The workspace uses firm section colour and exact tab hierarchy instead of floating cards.

options.label: Record Shop Index
options.lineage: independent record-shop shelf cards and listening-station catalogues
options.thesis: Sources behave like clearly indexed departments while the current record remains a small, tactile object in the shell.
options.viewport: A light catalogue workspace uses a blue index rail, compact track rows, and one square now-playing object in the titlebar popover.
options.risk: This is the most familiar music-catalogue direction and can feel like a polished library app rather than a distinctive Hermes tool.

options.label: Signal Wayfinding
options.thesis: Every source, destination, and playback state becomes a decision point the user can read in one glance.
options.viewport: A disciplined yellow titlebar popover points to Now Playing, Up Next, Browse, and Library while the workspace remains standard and task-led.
options.case: It wins immediate clarity and state recognition, but its committed yellow shell is louder than a player that stays beside conversation all day.
options.risk: Too much yellow competes with Hermes and turns a quiet dock into a permanent alert.

options.label: Focused Listening Wall
options.thesis: Artwork carries Browse while focus expands exactly one item and dims the surrounding catalogue.
options.viewport: A dark compact player sits above horizontal provider shelves; the focused item alone reveals details and actions.
options.case: It strongly identifies as music and makes discovery pleasant, but it is weaker for local-folder management and diagnostics.
options.risk: It can collapse into a generic streaming clone and overvalue artwork over source truth.

options.label: Section Manual
options.thesis: Browse, Library, Queue, and Settings become exact coloured divisions with layered states.
options.viewport: A precise tab rail frames a conventional Media workspace with one top layer for the active task.
options.case: The hierarchy is excellent, but the manual metaphor distances the product from listening and makes the titlebar surface feel over-authored.
options.kept: Firm section hierarchy and colour that owns real regions.
options.risk: Literal tabs and layered paper become costume rather than useful playback structure.

options.label: Mixtape J-Card
options.thesis: Up Next becomes a personal, timed listening sequence with strong ownership.
options.viewport: A compact queue reads like a handwritten tracklist beside a clean native player.
options.case: It identifies with personal listening but loses product clarity for Spotify devices, radio, folders, and provider errors.
options.kept: Make queue duration and sequence feel personally authored.
options.risk: Handwritten treatment becomes nostalgic decoration and weakens scanability.

canonCard.label: The category standard
canonCard.thesis: A familiar premium music app: dark shell, artwork grids, conventional player controls, executed cleanly.
canonCard.viewport: A standard sidebar, content grid, and bottom player translated carefully into Hermes.
canonCard.risk: Comfortable and clear, but indistinguishable from existing desktop music players.
